introduction-pets-vs-cattle.core: Pets are servers you name, patch and nurse back to health in place; each becomes unique over time. Cattle are identical, numbered and replaceable: if one is sick, you replace it. Immutable infrastructure takes cattle to its conclusion. You never modify a running server; you build a new image with the change and replace instances, so every server matches a known, tested artifact.

first_principles.problem: A critical server can't be rebuilt because nobody knows every change made to it over five years.

analogy.title: Repainting a car vs getting a new one from the factory
analogy.story: Every repaint adds unique blemishes; a factory car is identical to its test model.
analogy.breaks: Cars are expensive to replace; instances cost seconds.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Every server identical to the tested image.

check.q: What must be true of application state for immutable infrastructure to work?
check.a: It must live outside the instances (databases, object storage, EBS/EFS), so replacing an instance loses nothing.

packer-the-image-builder.core: HashiCorp Packer automates machine image builds. A source (builder) launches a temporary VM or container on a platform (amazon-ebs, azure-arm, googlecompute, docker), provisioners configure it (shell, Ansible, files), it is snapshotted into an image, and post-processors handle manifests and distribution. One template can build images for several platforms in parallel.

first_principles.problem: Images are built by clicking through the console, so no two are quite the same.
truths: Same config can target many platforms.

analogy.title: A cookie-cutter production line
analogy.story: Dough goes in, a temporary mould shapes it, and you get identical cookies every time.
analogy.breaks: Cookies don't need patching; images must be rebuilt regularly.

example.title: Build lifecycle
flow: packer build launches t3.small from base AMI

check.q: What happens to Packer's builder instance after the image is created?
check.a: It's terminated along with temporary keys and security groups; only the image artifact remains.

writing-a-packer-template.core: Modern Packer templates are HCL2 (*.pkr.hcl): a `packer` block pins plugins, `variable` blocks parameterise, a `source` block configures the builder (source_ami_filter, instance type, SSH user), and a `build` block lists sources and provisioners. Run `packer init`, `packer fmt`, `packer validate`, then `packer build`.

first_principles.problem: A legacy JSON template is hard to read and hardcodes the base AMI ID.

analogy.title: A recipe with substitutable ingredients
analogy.story: 'Latest flour from supplier X' rather than 'flour batch 12345'.
analogy.breaks: Recipes tolerate variance; builds should be deterministic given inputs.

check.q: Why use source_ami_filter instead of a fixed base AMI ID?
check.a: It picks up the latest patched base image automatically and works across regions where IDs differ.

golden-images-and-hardening.core: A golden image is the approved, hardened base for all workloads: OS patched, CIS benchmark settings applied, agents installed (logging, monitoring, EDR), unnecessary services removed. Teams build their app images on top of it. Bake hardening into the image and verify it with scanners (Inspec, OpenSCAP, Inspector), so every instance starts compliant instead of being fixed after launch.

first_principles.problem: Newly launched instances run for 30 minutes before a config agent hardens them, failing audits.

analogy.title: Pre-inspected building materials
analogy.story: Using certified materials means the building is compliant from day one, not after retrofits.
analogy.breaks: Materials don't go stale; images need regular rebuilds for patches.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Image fails to publish if baseline checks fail.

check.q: Why harden at image build time rather than at boot?
check.a: Instances are compliant from the first second, with no vulnerable window, and the result is tested once and reused.

ami-management-strategy.core: Images need lifecycle management: a regular rebuild cadence (weekly, or on CVE) for patches; a promotion pipeline (dev → staging → prod channels); sharing across accounts and regions; tracking which image each environment uses (HCP Packer channels or SSM parameters); and deregistering old AMIs and snapshots to control cost and prevent use of vulnerable images.

first_principles.problem: Production runs 14-month-old AMIs while 300 unused images and snapshots cost thousands per month.
truths: Old images cost money and carry CVEs.
derivation: Reference via **SSM parameter or HCP channel**.

analogy.title: Rotating stock in a supermarket
analogy.story: New stock goes to the back, shelves show what's approved, and expired items are removed.
analogy.breaks: Expired food is obvious; old AMIs look fine until scanned.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Promotion updates one parameter; next deploy rolls the new image.

check.q: Why reference AMIs via an SSM parameter or channel instead of hardcoding IDs?
check.a: Promotion becomes a single pointer update, and consumers always get the currently approved image without code changes.
